title: Visibility Bias in AI-Based Underwater Fish Monitoring: A Scoping Review of Ecological Validity and a Reporting Checklist
content: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly detects and counts fish in underwater imagery, but turbidity, light attenuation, low light, and distance affect which fish are visible. Ecology treats this as imperfect detection; the AI literature mostly treats it as an image-quality problem. This PRISMA-ScR scoping review coded 183 AI studies (2015–2026), identified through structured and database searches and evaluated on field-monitoring imagery from natural waters, on five dimensions of the observation process: visibility characterization, data independence, external-domain robustness, calibration and false-positive control, and ecological endpoint validation. A language model coded each study twice; the first author checked 90 studies (49%) against the full text, and the second author's blind coding of 40 randomly sampled studies agreed with 87% of its ratings. No study reported performance stratified by measured visibility, and only two measured water clarity with an instrument. Training and test data were separated by video, day, site, or region in 58 studies (32%); 18 (10%) compared the same model inside and outside its training domain; none reported a standard calibration metric; and 59 (32%) linked outputs to an ecological quantity, only 6 against a reference independent of the imagery. We propose a draft eleven-item reporting checklist (MRCUAI) and research agenda.
